The Show me page lets the reader **watch it happen**: written steps on the left,
an animated stage on the right, kept in sync. The player starts by itself when it
scrolls into view, because animations that play by themselves teach well. The
reader can pause, step back and forth, or click any step. In full mode a voice
button narrates each step and waits for the voice before moving on.

Add the page only when something actually happens: clicks in an app, commands in a
terminal, messages between systems or people, or a real screen whose look matters.
A page can hold one or two walkthroughs; more belong in separate explainers.

## The player

```html
<div class="walk">
  <div>
    <p class="kicker">On your screen</p>                         <!-- optional label -->
    <ol class="walk-steps">
      <li data-click=".u-new">Click <b>New token</b>.</li>
      <li data-click=".u-name" data-type="Build server" data-into=".u-name">Type a <b>name</b>.</li>
      <li data-ms="3500">It appears in the list.</li>
    </ol>
    <p class="walk-note">A simplified drawing of the screens, not a screenshot.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="walk-stage">
    …one stage: drawn screens, terminal, sequence or screenshot…
  </div>
</div>
```

The template adds the controls (back, play/pause, next, step count and progress
bar) under the stage. The steps are the real content: written for someone who
never presses play, with the screen's exact labels in **bold**.

**Step attributes** (on each `<li>`):

| Attribute | Effect |
|---|---|
| `data-click=".selector"` | the cursor glides to that element in the drawn screen and clicks it |
| `data-type="text"` + `data-into=".selector"` | types the text into that element (into its `.typed` child if it has one) |
| `data-ms="3500"` | how long the step stays when playing (default 3200 ms; steps with a click or typing wait until it's done). Every player time is multiplied by the page's pace (`--tempo`) |
| `data-box="x,y,w,h"` | screenshot tour: spotlight and zoom on that box (percentages of the image) |

**Stage attributes**, on any element inside the stage, tie it to the steps (steps
count from 0):

| Attribute | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `data-show="2"` | visible only on step 2. Ranges: `"1-3"`, `"3-"` (3 and later), `"-2"`, lists: `"0,5-"` |
| `data-on="2-"` | gets class `on` on those steps (style it in custom CSS) |
| `data-at="3"` | gets `now` on step 3 and `past` after it. Sequence rows use this |

## Stage A: drawn screens and a cursor

For anything done by clicking in an app or website. It's a simplified drawing, not
a screenshot: it shows only what matters, it can't go out of date pixel by pixel,
and it reads well on a phone. Name the real product, but don't copy its logo or
branding. Label buttons exactly as the product does.

```html
<div class="ui" style="--ui-h:400px" aria-hidden="true">
  <div class="ui-top">
    <span class="ui-logo"></span>
    <span class="ui-url" data-show="0-1">jira.example.com</span>      <!-- where you are, per step -->
    <span class="ui-dots"><i></i><i></i><i></i></span>
    <span class="ui-space"></span>
    <span class="ui-avatar u-avatar">A</span>
  </div>
  <div class="ui-body">
    <div class="ui-side" data-show="2-"><span>Summary</span><span class="on u-tokens">Personal access tokens</span></div>   <!-- optional side menu -->
    <div class="ui-main">
      <div class="ui-view" data-show="0-1">…a screen…</div>
      <div class="ui-view" data-show="2-">…the next screen…</div>
    </div>
  </div>
  <div class="ui-menu" data-show="1"><span class="on u-profile">Profile</span><span>Log out</span></div>
  <div class="ui-scrim" data-show="4-5"></div>
  <div class="ui-modal" data-show="4-5">…a dialog…</div>
</div>
```

Building blocks (all styled by the template):

| Class | What it draws |
|---|---|
| `ui-top`, `ui-logo`, `ui-url`, `ui-dots`, `ui-space`, `ui-avatar` | the top bar: a logo square, the address, placeholder menu items, a gap, the user's picture |
| `ui-body` > `ui-side` + `ui-main` | a side menu and the main area. Without `ui-side` the main area fills the width |
| `ui-view` | one screen inside the main area; give each a `data-show` |
| `ui-center` + `ui-panel` | a centred card, such as a sign-in box or a form |
| `ui-h` | a heading row (put a button at its end to align it right) |
| `ui-btn` (`ghost`, `go`) | buttons: dark, outlined, green |
| `ui-label` + `ui-input` | a form field; put `<span class="typed"></span><i class="caret"></i>` inside for typing |
| `ui-list` > `span` | rows such as accounts or settings (`<small>` for a second line) |
| `ui-row`, `ui-card`, `ui-grid`, `ui-lines` | a table row, a card, a grid of cards, grey placeholder text lines (`<i style="--w:60%"></i>`) |
| `ui-menu`, `ui-scrim`, `ui-modal`, `ui-actions` | a drop-down menu, the dimmed background, a dialog, its button row |
| `ui-hide-narrow` | hide this on phone widths |

Give every element the cursor clicks or types into a class starting with `u-`, and
point `data-click` / `data-into` at it. The cursor ripples orange and rings the
element when it clicks. On a phone the stage gets narrower (the side menu shrinks),
so keep each screen to the few things the step needs.

**Planning a drawn walkthrough:** list the steps first. For each, note the screen
before the click, the thing clicked, and what changes. Step *n*'s screen is the one
the reader sees *before* doing step *n*. Then draw one `ui-view` per distinct
screen and set `data-show` ranges. `assets/example-body.html` (page "show") has a
complete six-step sign-in walkthrough.

## Stage B: a terminal

For command-line procedures. Type each command with `data-type`, and reveal its
output on the next step:

```html
<div class="ui" style="--ui-h:300px" aria-hidden="true">
  <div class="ui-top"><span class="ui-logo"></span><span class="ui-url">Terminal</span></div>
  <div class="ui-body"><div class="ui-terminal">
    <div><span class="pr">$</span><span class="u-cmd1"><span class="typed"></span></span></div>
    <span class="out" data-show="1-">Cloning into 'project'… done.</span>
    <div data-show="1-"><span class="pr">$</span><span class="u-cmd2"><span class="typed"></span></span></div>
    <span class="out ok" data-show="2-">✓ 42 tests passed</span>
  </div></div>
</div>
```

Steps: `<li data-type="git clone https://…/project" data-into=".u-cmd1">Clone the project.</li>` (no `data-click`: a terminal needs no cursor, and the cursor only appears when some step clicks).
Copy commands exactly from the documentation, and show them in `<code>` in the
written step too, so readers can copy them.

- **Output** keeps its spaces and line breaks (useful for `git log --graph`). Put
  each block of output in its own `.out`, revealed with `data-show` from the step
  that produces it; `ok` colours a success line green.
- **The last command's output** needs one more step to appear. Make it a step to
  look at: "See the history: one straight line."
- **Height**: a terminal fits about 16 lines in `--ui-h:420px` (roughly 60px plus
  24px per line). Size it for the longest step, and keep output short: trim it to
  the lines that matter. The render check reports content taller than the screen.

## Stage C: a sequence

For messages between parties (people, browsers, servers, services). Use the
sequence diagram from diagrams.md and add `data-at` to each row. Rows appear one at
a time, the packet travels, and earlier rows fade back.

```html
<div class="stage-box d-seq" style="--lanes:3" aria-hidden="true">
  <div class="seq-actors">…</div>
  <div class="seq-rows">
    <div class="msg" data-at="0" style="--a:1;--b:0"><span class="line"></span><span class="lbl">sign me in</span><span class="pkt">click</span></div>
    <div class="msg direct" data-at="1" style="--a:0;--b:2"><span class="line"></span><span class="lbl">code + secret</span><span class="pkt">code</span></div>
  </div>
  <div class="seq-legend"><span>through your browser</span><span class="solid">direct</span></div>
</div>
```

Pair it with a drawn-screens walkthrough when the reader also needs to see what
happens behind the screen ("On your screen" and then "Behind the screen").

## Stage D: a screenshot tour

For when the real screen's look matters: recognising a page, finding a setting
among many, seeing a real result. The tour spotlights one area per step, zooms in
on it and numbers it.

```html
<div class="shot"><div class="shot-in"><img src="shots/settings.png" alt="The settings page of …"><span class="spot"></span><span class="pin">1</span></div></div>
```

Each step carries `data-box="x,y,w,h"`: the area's left, top, width and height
as percentages of the image. Small boxes zoom in more (up to 1.9×).

**Capturing the screenshots:**

- **With a browser tool** (Playwright or Claude in Chrome): open the page at a
  1280×760 window, take a viewport screenshot, and measure each area in the same
  view as percentages:
  ```js
  () => { const W = innerWidth, H = innerHeight;
    const box = s => { const r = document.querySelector(s).getBoundingClientRect();
      return [r.left / W * 100, r.top / H * 100, r.width / W * 100, r.height / H * 100].map(v => v.toFixed(1)).join(','); };
    return { save: box('button[type=submit]'), menu: box('nav') }; }
  ```
  If the tool saves files outside the work folder (for example into the
  repository), move them into `<work>/shots/` straight away and leave nothing behind.
- **Without one**: ask the user for screenshots, or use a drawn walkthrough instead.
- **Read every screenshot before using it.** Crop away anything personal (names,
  emails, tokens, customer data) or ask before publishing it. Prefer a drawn
  walkthrough when the real screen would expose private information.

## Before you ship a walkthrough

- Every step matches current official documentation (or the user's own system),
  and the labels are exact. Note the version or date in `.walk-note`.
- Every `data-click` and `data-into` selector exists in the stage; the build won't
  catch a typo, so watch the cursor in a browser if you can.
- At phone width every screen still fits and the clicked element is visible.
  render_check renders each walkthrough twice: on step 1, and on its last step
  (images tagged `-last`), and reports content taller than its drawn screen.
- The written steps make sense with the animation switched off.
